rewrites.summary:
Algeria is dangerous for trans visitors. Gender transition is not explicitly criminalised, but Cairo 52 documents that it is effectively criminalised through Penal Code Articles 333, 338, and 333 bis (indecency provisions), and NGOs have documented arrests of LGBT+ people under these articles. Same-sex activity itself carries up to 2 years under Article 338. There is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection, and no visible community infrastructure — activism operates almost entirely underground.

Unlike Tunisia or Morocco, Algeria lacks even a documented trans-visitor incident — partly because very few tourists visit and researchers have limited access. The legal exposure for a visibly trans visitor (indecency arrest) is real but the enforcement pattern is thinner than Egypt's entrapment machinery or Tunisia's 2024-25 arrest wave.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Same-sex activity carries up to 2 years under Article 338 — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Indecency-law application to trans people is documented in aggregate, not per-case; tourism volume is very low.

A government asylum report (26 Jul 2026, covering since May 2025): same-sex activity prohibited under the 1966 penal code; internal relocation viable for gay males but lesbians and trans females face societal difficulties; refusals rarely certifiable as clearly unfounded — the current asylum-authority baseline.

A fact-check (5 Aug 2024): rating TRUE — the country prohibits medical and surgical gender-affirming care and being transgender; published while debunking a false rumour about an athlete, confirming the ban is real even though the rumour was false.

A government annual human-rights report: law criminalised undefined 'homosexual acts' with 2 months' to 2 years' imprisonment plus fines; prison authorities separated vulnerable persons but LGBTQI+ detainees had no specific legal protections; civil society noted compounded discrimination for LGBTQI+ persons.

A 2008 report on government-sponsored homophobia: male/male and female/female relations illegal under the penal code (decree of 8 June 1966): 2 months' to 2 years' imprisonment and fines. Dated but the same law that a 2026 government report confirms is still in force.

A human-rights organisation (15 Oct 2020): after a raid on a private home, police arrested 44 people over an alleged 'gay wedding'; a court sentenced some to prison and the rest to suspended terms, using decorations and 'gay appearance' as evidence.

A survey (23 Jun 2019, 25,000 respondents across 10 countries): this country was the exception where fewer than 50% accepted a woman head of government; region-wide, 'not religious' identification rose from 8% to 13% since 2013 — social-conservatism context datum for the record.

rewrites.summary:
Tunisia is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — the country is in an active crackdown. Between 26 September 2024 and 31 January 2025, authorities arrested at least 84 people in Tunis, Hammamet, Sousse and El Kef on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity — mostly gay men and transgender women, per Amnesty International. Penal Code Articles 226 bis (public indecency) and 230 (sodomy, up to 3 years) are applied to effectively criminalise gender expression, and enforcement disproportionately targets transgender women.

In detention, trans women are processed under birth names and housed in men's prisons, where local NGO Intersection documents severe abuse. The courts have hardened: in April 2023 the Tunis Court of First Instance refused legal gender recognition to a trans man, dismissing gender dysphoria as “mental illness.” Since President Saied's 2021 power consolidation, the post-revolution space for LGBT organising (Shams, Damj) has been crushed — Shams was dissolved.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Article 230 (sodomy, up to 3 years) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners; the 2024-25 arrest wave explicitly included trans women on gender-identity grounds.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is statutory context; the 2024-25 wave explicitly targeted trans women on gender-identity grounds.
rewrites.blindSummary:

Penal-code articles on public indecency and sodomy (up to 3 years) are applied to effectively criminalise gender expression, and enforcement disproportionately targets transgender women.

In detention, trans women are processed under birth names and housed in men's prisons, where a local organisation documents severe abuse. The courts have hardened: in April 2023 a first-instance court refused legal gender recognition to a trans man, dismissing gender dysphoria as “mental illness.” Since the 2021 consolidation of power, the space for LGBT organising has been crushed — one group was dissolved.

rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Same-sex criminalisation is statutory context; the 2024-25 wave explicitly targeted trans women on gender-identity grounds.
blindSourceSummaries: A human-rights organisation (11 Feb 2025): at least 84 people — mainly gay men and trans women — arrested, arbitrarily detained and prosecuted between 26 Sep 2024 and 31 Jan 2025 on 'public indecency'/morality charges; a 31 Oct 2024 mass conviction drew prison terms up to 4.5 years, upheld on appeal 5 Feb 2025. Quantified 2024-25 crackdown evidence.

An organisation's country page: a penal article criminalises same-sex conduct with up to 3 years' imprisonment; records enforcement (e.g. an Oct 2021 arrest of two transgender women under morality provisions) and gaps in legal gender recognition. Primary-law summary for visitor risk.

A local organisation (Nov 2024): transgender women in the country's prisons are processed under their former names and birth gender in detention records, arrest processes and court hearings — systemic identity refusal from detention onward, described as continuous suffering and discrimination inside the prison system. Direct trans-specific custodial-risk evidence.

An organisation (30 Jan 2024): reports a first-instance court's Apr 2023 refusal of legal gender recognition to a transgender man; the court weighed contradictory lower-court judgements and found no consistent precedent, leaving recognition unsettled below the highest court. Shows legal gender recognition is court-by-court and often denied.

A human-rights organisation (29 Mar 2016): documents at least seven men prosecuted for consensual same-sex conduct in two cases over six months, all convicted under a penal-code article (up to 3 years); interviewed detainees reported beatings, forced examinations and humiliating treatment by police. Core enforcement-abuse evidence.

A media report (27 Sep 2017): the country pledged to a world body to stop forced testing in same-sex cases, but kept the anti-gay law itself; another outlet warns the pledge does not decriminalise anything. Shows reform-by-commitment without legal change.

rewrites.summary:
Cameroon is dangerous for trans visitors. The Shakiro case is the defining documentation: in February 2021, trans women Shakiro and Patricia were arrested in a Douala restaurant for the clothes they were wearing, convicted of “attempted homosexuality,” “indecent dressing” and ID irregularities, and sentenced to five years. They described five months of “hell” in Douala's central prison, initially in leg chains, before release pending appeal; Shakiro later received asylum in Belgium. Article 347-1 criminalises same-sex acts (up to 5 years), and Cameroon has among Africa's highest prosecution rates.

Police and mob violence against perceived LGBT people are both documented, and there is no legal gender recognition or protection of any kind. The Shakiro conviction shows that visible trans expression in a public place is itself treated as a prosecutable offence.

For a visitor: visible trans presentation in public risks arrest on indecency/ID grounds; prison conditions are severe.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Article 347-1 criminalises same-sex acts (up to 5 years) — the vehicle for the Shakiro convictions and a direct risk for trans visitors with partners.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is the statutory vehicle; the Shakiro case demonstrates direct application to gender expression.

blindSourceSummaries: A news outlet (12 May 2021): a court jailed a trans woman and her friend for five years under 'attempted homosexuality' plus fines each — the maximum statutory term — with appeal filed; detained since February 2021. Lawyers called it a political decision with no proof of acts. Notes the national 2016 penal code explicitly outlawed same-sex relations, one of 31 countries criminalising, with beatings of gay/trans people common in public.

A biography of the trans activist: gained online following discussing trans life; arrested and charged with 'attempted homosexuality' in 2021, sentenced to five years, subsequently fled the country and claimed asylum abroad. Biographical corroboration of the 2021 case and its outcome (exile), tracking the human-rights profile of the criminalisation cases.

A government 2010 human-rights report: documents discrimination against gays and lesbians among societal abuses, alongside security-force killings, torture, harsh prisons, and arbitrary arrests — the criminalisation context.

A human-rights organisation (11 May 2022): documented a 2022 uptick of violence against LGBTI people — since March, security forces arbitrarily arrested at least 6 and detained 11 people, all victims of group attacks, for alleged consensual same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity; officers beat two in detention. Frames the pattern: the criminalisation law lets both civilians and security forces abuse LGBTI people without consequence.

A news outlet (9 Jan 2013): an appeals court acquitted two men jailed five years in November 2011 solely because they wore women's clothes — the original judge had cited dress and speech as proof they were gay. Conviction rested on stereotypes with no observed acts. Establishes the pattern: arrests on appearance grounds under a historic-era sodomy law with six-month-to-five-year sentences.

rewrites.summary:
Tanzania is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. The Penal Code criminalises same-sex activity with up to life imprisonment, and the political environment has been actively hostile since the Magufuli-era crackdowns (arrests, forced anal examinations documented by HRW in earlier years, de-registration of LGBT-serving organisations). The 2024 case of Mauzinde is emblematic: a transgender woman and activist found abandoned in a forest in Rahaleo, beaten, her ears cut off — an attack the UN Human Rights Office called “horrendous.”

OONI documented extensive targeted blocking of LGBTQ websites correlating with the escalating crackdown, and Amnesty's 2024 regional report notes Tanzanian pushes to further criminalise LGBT people. Zanzibar has its own, harsher penal code. There is no legal gender recognition and no protection infrastructure.

For a visitor: visible trans presentation risks arrest under indecency provisions and mob violence; Zanzibar is worse than the mainland.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Same-sex activity criminalised with up to life imprisonment — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Life-imprisonment statute is same-sex (climate/situational); the Mauzinde attack is trans-specific.
rewrites.blindSummary:

The penal code criminalises same-sex activity with up to life imprisonment, and the political environment has been actively hostile since earlier crackdowns (arrests, forced examinations documented by a human-rights organisation in earlier years, de-registration of LGBT-serving organisations). The 2024 case is emblematic: a transgender woman and activist found abandoned in a forest, beaten, her ears cut off — an attack a human-rights office called “horrendous.”

Targeted blocking of LGBTQ websites was documented, correlating with the escalating crackdown, and a 2024 regional report notes national pushes to further criminalise LGBT people. One part of the country has its own, harsher penal code. There is no legal gender recognition and no protection infrastructure.

For a visitor: visible trans presentation risks arrest under indecency provisions and mob violence; that part is worse than the rest of the country.

rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Life-imprisonment statute is same-sex (climate/situational); the attack is trans-specific.
blindSourceSummaries: A legal-news outlet (9 Jun 2024): a human-rights office condemned as 'horrendous' the attack on a transgender activist — abducted by 12 men, found beaten in a forest with her ears cut — calling for 'bold action to combat discrimination against LGBTIQ+ people'; it flagged possible violations of international and constitutional equality guarantees.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time; an underlying country profile documents the country's criminalisation of same-sex activity (life imprisonment possible).

A 2024 report on online censorship: documents the blocking of LGBTIQ websites and other targeted blocks based on measurement data — including LGBTIQ social networks and rights sites — evidencing government-directed online filtering that constrains LGBT access to information.

A human-rights organisation's report (Jan 2024): documents escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment and the weaponisation of law against LGBTI people, with legislation on same-sex relations deferred after protests, in a documented climate of discrimination limiting rights enjoyment — national-level findings.

Interview (4 Sep 2020) with three anonymised local LGBT activists: documents substantial prejudice, discrimination and violence against LGBT people and denial of basic rights, with homophobia and transphobia driving the urgency of rights advocacy; includes definitions of sexual orientation, gender identity and trans woman terms.

A 2004 penal decree (full text): enacted by the sub-national legislature; defines 'gross indecency' broadly as any sexual act falling short of intercourse, sets sexual-offence age thresholds (absolute under 12; under-18 and marriage distinctions) and penalties including imprisonment for three years — criminal law applying to one part of the country alongside national law.

A government 2013 human-rights report: the three most widespread problems were security-force excessive force, gender-based violence, and lack of access to justice; also 'discrimination based on sexual orientation' and societal violence.

rewrites.summary:
Ethiopia is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex activity is criminalised (up to 1 year, or more under aggravating provisions), and because Ethiopia has no legal gender recognition, trans people are legally treated as their birth sex — meaning a trans person's ordinary relationships can be prosecuted as same-sex conduct. The 2024 UPR stakeholder report documents discrimination, violence, and absence of police protection, with trans women and queer women particularly at risk, plus a growing organised anti-LGBTQ+ campaign inside the country.

Documented trans-specific enforcement is thinner than Cameroon's or Tunisia's — Ethiopia's LGBTQ+ community (self-identified as “zega”) is deeply underground, and reporting is sparse — but the legal structure (criminalisation + no LGR catch-all), hostile campaigning, and absence of any protection place it clearly on the dangerous side of the scale. Digital surveillance and blackmail vulnerability are noted in the UPR reporting.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Same-sex criminalisation (up to 1 year, more under aggravation) — because there is no LGR, a trans person's relationships are legally same-sex; a direct mechanism, not merely climate.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation captures trans people via birth-sex legal status — a direct, not situational, mechanism.
rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex activity is criminalised (up to 1 year, or more under aggravating provisions), and because the country has no legal gender recognition, trans people are legally treated as their birth sex — meaning a trans person's ordinary relationships can be prosecuted as same-sex conduct. The 2024 report documents discrimination, violence, and absence of police protection, with trans women and queer women particularly at risk, plus a growing organised anti-LGBTQ+ campaign inside the country.

Documented trans-specific enforcement is thinner — the national LGBTQ+ community is deeply underground and reporting is sparse — but the legal structure (criminalisation with no recognition catch-all), hostile campaigning, and absence of any protection place it clearly on the dangerous side of the scale. Digital surveillance and blackmail vulnerability are noted in the reporting.
rewrites.blindTangential: Same-sex criminalisation (up to 1 year, more under aggravation) — because there is no legal gender recognition, a trans person's relationships are legally same-sex; a direct mechanism, not merely climate.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Same-sex criminalisation captures trans people via birth-sex legal status — a direct, not situational, mechanism.
blindSourceSummaries: Stakeholder submission to a periodic review: same-sex activity criminalised, leaving LGBTQ+ people at serious risk of harm and systematic exclusion; discrimination, violence, lack of police protection and stigma in services; no legal gender change — trans men are legally women and trans women legally men, so trans people in different-gender relationships can fall foul of the same-sex conduct law.

A stakeholder report (April 2024) on gender identity and expression: documents discrimination, violence, and lack of protection; notes transgender people are particularly at risk given the criminalisation framework.

A barometer country profile, time series 2011-2024 (all years scored 'no' on every protection axis): no legal gender recognition (neither surgical nor psychiatric pathway exists), no hate-speech or hate-crime legislation covering gender identity, no freedom from arbitrary arrest based on gender identity/expression, LGBTI organisations cannot register, events not allowed and participants unprotected, no workplace or housing discrimination protections including gender identity.
A government 2008 human-rights report (archived): documents the criminalisation of same-sex conduct and societal stigma — baseline country-of-origin information.

A government 2011 human-rights report (archived): documents arrests of opposition figures, civil-society-law restrictions on civil society, and the LGBT section noting criminalisation and societal discrimination.

A government 2010 human-rights report: documents the anti-terrorism prosecutions, civil-society-law restrictions, torture, harsh prisons — general context with the LGBT section noting criminalisation.

A university thesis (2009): analyses the construction of homosexuality in relation to gender; male homosexuality criminalised (up to 3 years); media and elites create homophobia in discourse; a religious institution effectively campaigns hatred; female homosexuality simply overlooked; attitudes shifting under globalisation.

A rights organisation's country overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): a 2004 criminal-code article outlaws same-sex conduct between men and between women — rarely enforced but underpinning pervasive anti-LGBTIQ stigma, harassment and violence; in August 2023 security forces cracked down on 'homosexuality' while non-government actors drove an online incitement wave ending in physical attacks; religious groups campaign for harsher penalties. A charities law blocks registration of LGBTI groups as 'contrary to public morality'. At a glance: same-sex relations illegal nationwide, no legal gender recognition, LGBTI organisations cannot register.

A government 2023 human-rights report: criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct drives near-total concealment of identity — individuals generally do not publicly identify as LGBTQI+; activists report surveillance, entrapment and fear for their safety, with harassment/violence increasing toward end of 2023. High levels of societal discrimination nationwide in education, employment and healthcare; being outed risks physical violence and ostracism. Authoritative annual baseline for government and social risk to a trans visitor.

rewrites.summary:
Lebanon is dangerous for trans visitors — the Arab world's most socially open country layered over one of its most explicitly anti-trans statutes. Article 521 of the Penal Code prescribes up to six years' imprisonment for “men disguising themselves as women” — a direct criminalisation of trans feminine expression. Article 534 (“intercourse contrary to the order of nature,” up to 1 year) remains in force though several courts have ruled it inapplicable to same-sex relations. Courts have granted legal gender recognition in some post-surgery cases since 1987, but inconsistently.

Beirut's queer scene is the region's most visible — bars, NGOs (Helem, Proud Lebanon), and a documented court history — but the climate deteriorated sharply since 2022: state-affiliated militia groups attacked queer venues after an anti-discrimination bill was introduced, and Cairo 52 documents rising prejudice and violence against trans people, particularly trans women, who face entrenched marginalisation and family/community violence.

For a visitor: Beirut is navigable with discretion; visible trans feminine expression carries real (statutory) arrest risk; the economic collapse has degraded police predictability in both directions.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Article 534 ("intercourse contrary to the order of nature," up to 1 year) — a situational risk for trans visitors with partners, though several courts have ruled it inapplicable to same-sex relations.
rewrites.localsOnly: The case-by-case post-surgery LGR rulings and healthcare pathologisation are resident-facing.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: LGR case law and healthcare pathologisation are resident-facing; Art 521/534 are the traveler-relevant statutes.

blindSourceSummaries: An organisation's country review: the country employs both de facto and explicit criminalisation to penalise transgender expression, particularly targeting transgender women; a rise in prejudice and violence against trans and queer people is documented in its main city, including incidents responding to a decriminalisation bill tabled in parliament; gradual legal-gender-recognition progress since 2015 when a judge approved a plaintiff's gender-marker change on identity documents.

An asylum country-of-origin report (fetched 2026-09-29): dedicated section on LGBTIQ persons including activists — treats LGBTIQ claims as a distinct risk category with defined terms of reference and source methodology.

A human-rights organisation (8 Apr 2022): regional dispatch — countries in the region should ensure access to legal gender recognition; documents trans people's exposure to policing and documentation barriers alongside neighbouring countries.

A magazine report (Mar 2022): maps regional case law on legal gender recognition — the national judiciary has a long history of reviewing trans plaintiffs' name/marker changes governed by the civil registry code of 1951, with an earlier precedent and heavy roles for medical and religious authorities; compares the country with several regional peers.

A rights organisation's country overview (updated Mar 2026), at-a-glance: same-sex relations for men and for women are not legal throughout the country; legal gender recognition not possible (overview page cached truncated; article-level detail not retrievable in cache).

A human-rights organisation (18 May 2018): security forces arrested a prominent LGBT rights activist and pressured him to cancel a planned public event in the main city — nine days of LGBT-identity activities — in a crackdown called a violation of freedom of assembly and a step backward for LGBT rights.

A media profile (15 May 2018): a local LGBT rights advocate helped create a long-standing advocacy group and later led a regional foundation, campaigning for LGBT equality across hostile regional countries.

A human-rights organisation (2 Feb 2017): a ruling pushed the country closer to decriminalising same-sex conduct, following the 2009 precedent that consensual same-sex conduct is not a criminal offence.
